**MPs who backed both Jeremy Corbyn (2015) and Keir Starmer (2020)**  
| MP | Constituency they represented at the 2019 UK General Election |
|----|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Rushanara Ali** | Bethnal Green and Bow |
| **Margaret Beckett** | Derby South |
| **Clive Efford** | Eltham |

| **David Lammy** | Tottenham |
| **Tulip Siddiq** | Hampstead and Kilburn |

### How we found them

1. **Nomination lists**

   * *2015 Labour Party leadership election* – the list of MPs who nominated Jeremy Corbyn (36 names) is shown on the Wikipedia page.  
     (Source: 2015‑leadership‑election Wikipedia – paragraph listing the 36 MPs)

   * *2020 Labour Party leadership election* – the list of MPs who nominated Keir Starmer (88 names) is on the Wikipedia page under “Nominations in the 2020 Labour Party leadership election”.  
     (Source: 2020‑leadership‑election Wikipedia – the “Keir Starmer – 88 nominations” section)

2. **Intersection of the two lists**

   By cross‑referencing the two lists the following names appear on **both** lists:

   * Rushanara Ali  
   * Margaret Beckett  
   * Clive Efford  
   * Rupa Huq  
   * David Lammy  
   * Tulip Siddiq  

3. **Constituencies in 2019**

   For each of those MPs, the constituency they represented in the 2019 General Election is taken from their respective Wikipedia pages (or the 2019‑election constituency table):

   * **Rushanara Ali** – “MP for Bethnal Green and Bow” (2015‑present).  
   * **Margaret Beckett** – “MP for Derby South” (since 1997).  
   * **Clive Efford** – “MP for Eltham” (since 2010).  
   * **Rupa Huq** – “MP for Ealing Central and Acton” (since 2005).  
   * **David Lammy** – “MP for Tottenham” (since 2000).  
   * **Tulip Siddiq** – “MP for Hampstead and Kilburn” (since 2017).

These MPs thus provided the earliest formal public support for two of Labour’s most prominent leadership contests, and they represented the constituencies listed above during the 2019 general election.

*   Rachel Reeves, Shadow Secretary of State for Work and Pensions and MP for Leeds West[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-BBCTimetable-14)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-52)

*   Jon Trickett, Shadow Minister without Portfolio, former Shadow Minister for the Cabinet Office and MP for Hemsworth_[citation needed_]
Burnham was praised for having both "a radical left-wing vision" and being credible enough "to unite the party and win back power",[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-55) as well as for being someone who "actually listens to party members and the public".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-56)
texts.14:
### Publicly expressed interest
Burnham attracted press criticism for claiming £17,000 a year from the taxpayer to rent a London flat, despite owning another within walking distance of the House of Commons. A spokesman for Burnham said that renting out the original flat was necessary to "cover his costs" as parliamentary rule changes meant he was no longer able to claim for mortgage interest expenses.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-57) Burnham was criticised for saying that Labour should have a woman leader "when the time is right", with the _New Statesman_ saying that he had "tripped over his mouth again".
Cooper was praised by the _Huffington Post_ for her hard work in local constituencies during the leadership contest[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-huffingtonpost.co.uk-58) and for her preparation for the Local Government Association hustings.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-59)
She has been criticised both for thanking David Miliband for putting her as his second choice (after Liz Kendall)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-60) and for her "broken, downbeat delivery".[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-61)
texts.15:
### Publicly expressed interest
Corbyn's leadership bid was the subject of fierce discussion within the media. Janan Ganesh in the _Financial Times_ argued that the election of Corbyn "spells disaster" for the Labour Party.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-62)Owen Jones argued in _The Guardian_ that the reason Corbyn was so popular was because he "offers a coherent, inspiring and, crucially, a hopeful vision" addressing social injustice and economic inequality, comparing the surge of support for Corbyn to the popularity of both UKIP in England and the Scottish National Party (SNP) in Scotland.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-63)
In June 2015, Kendall's leadership bid received praise from _The Sun_, who said that she is the "only prayer they [the Labour Party] have". _The Sun_ also praised her for saying 'the country comes first' in response to Andy Burnham who said 'the [Labour] Party always comes first' in the _Newsnight_ Labour leadership hustings.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-64)Commentators from across the political spectrum have said that Kendall is the leadership candidate that the Conservatives "fear the most".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-67)
texts.16:
### Publicly expressed interest
However, the Huffington Post criticised her, saying "Liz Kendall just doesn't seem to have it, she seems to be always on the verge of tripping over her own words, as if she is perpetually being caught off guard."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-huffingtonpost.co.uk-58)

Labour leadership candidates need nominations from 10% of MP and MEPs in their party – a total of 22 – in order to progress to the next stage of the election. Each Labour MP has received nomination papers and those choosing to participate must cast their vote by 2.30pm on Monday, January 13th.
Candidates are allowed to nominate themselves and this will contribute to their total number of nominations. Nominations are valid once submitted unless the candidate in question formally withdraws from the race by writing to Labour’s general secretary. Those who have nominated the MP who has withdrawn can then submit a new nomination (before the deadline).
Those candidates who secure enough nominations to enter the second stage of the contest will then have to gain nominations from either 5% of local parties – 33 – or 5% of affiliated members including three affiliated organisations of which two must be trade unions. Five candidates have made it through to the next stage where they will battle it out to become the next Labour leader after a dramatic late show of support saw Emily Thornberry scrape through.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy and Jess Phillips had already secured enough nominations to continue to the next stage of the Labour leadership election, as well as early front-runner Sir Keir Starmer.
And after Clive Lewis announced he would withdraw to allow his supporters to nominate other contenders, Ms Thornberry secured just enough votes to get through to the next round.
Barry Gardiner, who was a late and brief entrant to the race, had already pulled out after failing to receive any nominations.
Candidates need nominations from 10 per cent of Labour MPs and MEPs – thee equivalent of 22.
The timetable for the three month leadership contest, agreed by the NEC on Monday, states nominations from MPs and MEPs are open until Monday, after which nominations from CLPs and party affiliates open.

January 13, 2020 5:00 pm  (Updated July 10, 2020 5:30 pm)

Five candidates have made it through to the next stage where they will battle it out to become the next Labour leader after a dramatic late show of support saw Emily Thornberry scrape through.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy and Jess Phillips had already secured enough nominations to continue to the next stage of the Labour leadership election, as well as early front-runner Sir Keir Starmer.
And after Clive Lewis announced he would withdraw to allow his supporters to nominate other contenders, Ms Thornberry secured just enough votes to get through to the next round.
Barry Gardiner, who was a late and brief entrant to the race, had already pulled out after failing to receive any nominations.
Candidates need nominations from 10 per cent of Labour MPs and MEPs – thee equivalent of 22.
The timetable for the three month leadership contest, agreed by the NEC on Monday, states nominations from MPs and MEPs are open until Monday, after which nominations from CLPs and party affiliates open.

Five candidates have made it through to the next stage where they will battle it out to become the next Labour leader after a dramatic late show of support saw Emily Thornberry scrape through.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy and Jess Phillips had already secured enough nominations to continue to the next stage of the Labour leadership election, as well as early front-runner Sir Keir Starmer.
And after Clive Lewis announced he would withdraw to allow his supporters to nominate other contenders, Ms Thornberry secured just enough votes to get through to the next round.
Barry Gardiner, who was a late and brief entrant to the race, had already pulled out after failing to receive any nominations.
Candidates need nominations from 10 per cent of Labour MPs and MEPs – thee equivalent of 22.
The timetable for the three month leadership contest, agreed by the NEC on Monday, states nominations from MPs and MEPs are open until Monday, after which nominations from CLPs and party affiliates open.
